title: The power to impose conditions — and its legal limits
paras: Let's start with the power to impose conditions — and where it stops. An authority can grant permission subject to whatever conditions it thinks fit, but it's fenced in by the supplementary statutory provisions, the common-law tests, and national policy; the citations stay in the written guide. Two express statutory powers: conditioning land under the applicant's control beyond the red line where expedient, and requiring works removed or a use stopped after a set period — temporary permissions. Default time limits sit here too: three years to begin a full permission, and the twin limits on an outline.

The legality tests come from Newbury: a condition must serve a genuine planning purpose, not an ulterior one; must fairly and reasonably relate to the development permitted; and mustn't be so unreasonable no reasonable authority could impose it. Fail any and it's ultra vires. The reach is wide, mind — a condition can serve almost any purpose that falls within the scope of the planning Acts — but those three tests are the fence around that width. These predate the policy tests and survive alongside them — one goes to legality, the other to soundness.

If a condition's void, the question is severance — strike it and leave the permission, or is it so fundamental the permission falls too? Courts split fundamental from incidental, but nobody litigates it; the working route is a section seventy-three, which asks cleanly and preserves the permission either way. So three layers run through every conditions problem: statute, what can lawfully be required; common law, whether the condition is valid; policy, whether it should have been imposed. Most arguments are policy dressed as legal, and spotting the right layer fixes the remedy and its deadline.

title: The six tests and the policy framework
paras: Now the six tests. Policy keeps conditions to a minimum and imposes them only where all six hold: necessary; relevant to planning; relevant to the development permitted; enforceable; precise; reasonable in all other respects. One needing discharge before you start should be avoided without clear justification. And a prior principle: a condition can make acceptable what would otherwise be refused, so you reach for an obligation only where a condition can't do the job.

Each fails differently. Necessary — the permission would have to be refused without it, so a merely desirable one, or one restating what the applicant would do anyway, fails. Relevant to planning is the first Newbury limb: no collateral objectives, no duplicating another regime. Relevant to the development permitted stops using a house extension to lever works out of unrelated land. Enforceable — could a breach be detected and remedied? One depending on a third party the applicant can't compel dies here, so positive third-party obligations go into a section one-oh-six. Precise — the applicant can read it and know exactly what's required; 'to the satisfaction of the authority', with no objective standard, is the classic offender, and it matters doubly against a criminal-enforcement backdrop. Reasonable in all other respects is the residual Wednesbury limb — no unjustifiable or disproportionate cost.

One point on lineage, for older permissions: the tests began in the old 1995 circular, cancelled in England in 2014 when the practice guidance took over — superseded, though still cited and its model conditions still circulate. Wales kept the substance in its own circular, one of several divergences.

title: Categories of condition
paras: Categories now — because when a condition bites drives both how you discharge it and what breach costs. Pre-commencement conditions — conditions precedent — stop development until a requirement's met; the giveaway is 'no development shall take place until' something's submitted and approved in writing. Dangerous ones: breaching a true condition precedent can mean the permission was never lawfully implemented — the Whitley principle, its own topic.

Then conditions reserving approval of details — materials, landscaping, drainage, a construction management plan. They don't necessarily stop you starting; whether one also bars commencement turns on its precise wording, not its subject — the same drainage condition can be routine on one permission and void implementation on another, purely on drafting. Occupancy and use conditions control who occupies — the agricultural occupancy condition — or tie use to a class, or remove permitted development rights; those removal conditions are read strictly and must be precise, and a blanket removal without justification is vulnerable. Temporary conditions require a use to stop or works removed after a period, and the guidance warns against repeated temporary permissions and demolition conditions on permanent buildings.

And Grampian conditions — negative ones prohibiting development until something happens, often off-site, sometimes on land the applicant doesn't control; the accepted way to secure what a positive condition couldn't lawfully demand. The Grampian case established them; a later Court of Appeal decision relaxed the old 'reasonable prospects' requirement. So one isn't objectionable just because compliance looks unlikely — though the authority can still refuse where there's no reasonable prospect of it happening within the life of the permission.

title: What a condition cannot require — and the s100ZA control
paras: What a condition simply cannot do: make an applicant give up land or rights. The Supreme Court settled that in DB Symmetry — a condition can't require a landowner to dedicate land as public highway or grant rights over its own land, confirming the old Shoreham principle that an authority can't use a condition to extract, for nothing, what it would otherwise have to buy. And because the case turned on construction, an ambiguous condition of this kind is read down so it doesn't impose an unlawful positive obligation — drafting is decisive.

Anything of that character — dedication, transfer, payment, grant of rights — must be secured by agreement: a section one-oh-six or a highways agreement. Otherwise the choice between condition and obligation runs on the same necessity logic plus the community infrastructure levy test — necessary, directly related, fairly and reasonably related in scale and kind. The default, reinforced by policy, is that whatever can be done by condition should be — cheaper, quicker, no deed. Obligations earn their place only where a condition would fail on enforceability or reasonableness: positive obligations, financial contributions, control beyond the red line.

There's also a procedural control on pre-commencement conditions. Since 2018 an authority in England can't impose one without the applicant's written agreement, unless a statutory exception applies. If negotiation fails it serves notice of the proposed condition in full with reasons; the applicant then has at least ten working days to respond. Written agreement lets it through, a substantive objection blocks it, silence lets the authority proceed. That forces pre-commencement substance to the front and lets applicants turn a hard bar into a condition that merely reserves details. But it controls imposition only — it doesn't soften the legal effect once the condition is validly imposed, and it doesn't reach reserved matters on an outline in the ordinary way.

title: Discharge: the article 27 machinery
paras: Discharge. Three operations get loosely called 'dealing with conditions', and keeping them apart matters for fees, timing and legal effect: discharge — approving the details — satisfies a condition and leaves the permission untouched; varying or removing a condition produces a fresh permission; a non-material amendment tweaks the existing one. This topic is the first.

There's no free-standing 'application to discharge a condition' in the Act — you apply for the approval the condition calls for, and the decision records the reserved details as approved, it doesn't amend the condition. Three consequences: it doesn't touch the permission or its time limit, so approving details out of time won't revive a lapsed permission; the authority is confined to what the condition reserved, so it can't reopen the principle or add requirements; and a refusal is appealable. To be valid it must identify the permission and condition, include the particulars and plans, and carry the right fee — no fee, no clock. Determination is eight weeks from the day after a valid application lands — sixteen for environmental impact assessment development — extendable only by written agreement. One request can cover several conditions, and partial discharge by phase, plot or part of a condition is routine.

Fees are per request, not per condition — from April 2026, eighty-nine pounds on a householder permission, three hundred and nine otherwise, biodiversity gain plan conditions included. Bundle several into one submission and you pay once; drip-feed and you pay each time. If the authority misses the deadline the fee-refund provisions may bite, but the refund trigger and the determination deadline don't line up, so track them separately. And on a pre-commencement condition, sequence is everything — discharge only lifts the bar if you get it before you start; approval after works begin doesn't cure the breach of a true condition precedent. The Whitley line polices the order of events, not just the substance.

title: Deemed discharge: the self-help remedy
paras: Deemed discharge is the self-help answer to an authority that sits on your application. Where it applies, a condition needing approval is treated as discharged if the authority fails to determine your discharge application in time and you follow the notice procedure — from the Infrastructure Act reforms about a decade ago. The mechanism is sequential: a valid application first; then, no earlier than six weeks after the authority received it — or a shorter agreed period — you serve a deemed discharge notice identifying the application and conditions and confirming you haven't appealed. The condition is discharged on the later of two dates: expiry of the statutory determination period, and fourteen days after the authority gets your notice. With no decision by then, you proceed as if the details were approved as applied for.

But the regime carves out the sensitive ground — unavailable for environmental impact assessment or habitats cases; flood risk, contaminated land, sites of special scientific interest; highways matters needing an agreement, or any condition requiring a section one-oh-six or a highways agreement; archaeology; reserved matters on an outline; development under a development order; and Crown development. And the parties can agree in writing to switch it off entirely.

So it's used sparingly — unavailable for exactly the conditions where delay is most common, and on self-certified details you carry the risk of being wrong. An authority served with a notice may argue the regime never applied — a carve-out, an invalid underlying application so time never ran, or a defective notice. And a developer who builds on a deemed discharge later found ineffective is where one who never discharged stands: in breach — and if the condition was a true precedent, possibly with no implemented permission.

title: Changing the condition: s73, s96A — and the coming s73B
paras: When the client wants a condition changed or deleted, not satisfied, the route is a section seventy-three — permission to develop without complying with a condition already imposed. The authority can grant on different conditions, grant unconditionally, or refuse. Two fundamentals: the grant is a new, free-standing permission alongside the original — you implement either, and the original survives unless it lapses; and the authority is confined to the conditions in question, so it can't reopen the principle, though it applies the development plan and material considerations as at the section seventy-three decision date, not the original.

The decisive limit is Finney: a section seventy-three can't alter the description of development in the operative part of the permission. Within that the power is generous — even substantial changes by varying conditions, provided you don't contradict the description. But watch the drafting trap: the new permission is read as a whole, and any condition the parties forgot to carry across won't be read back in, even an obvious slip — left off the notice, it's gone. Fees from April 2026: eighty-nine pounds householder, six hundred and eight non-major, two thousand and seventy-six major.

The non-material amendment is the modest sibling — no new permission, a twenty-eight-day determination, and it can touch the description where the change is genuinely non-material. There's no statutory definition; it's fact and degree against the specific permission, and the authority can't stray into wider merits. Fees from April 2026: forty-six pounds householder, three hundred and nine otherwise. It's for drafting slips and minor dimensional changes, and it's habitually overreached — approving a genuinely material change this way is challengeable and no foundation to build on.

And a new power is coming, to fill the gap Finney exposed: varying a permission, description included, where the result is 'not substantially different' from what was permitted. As at mid-2026 it's not in force — awaiting commencement regulations and a fee framework. Until then: description untouched, section seventy-three; genuinely trivial, a non-material amendment; anything else, a fresh application.

title: Disputes: appeals, enforcement and the Whitley principle
paras: Finally, disputes. A refusal or non-determination of a discharge application carries a right of appeal — almost always written representations, confined to whether the details should have been approved. A condition itself you attack on appeal against the grant, or by section seventy-three with an appeal if refused. The choice matters: on a straight appeal the Inspector can treat the whole application as if made to him fresh, so appealing one condition throws the entire permission open — rarely disturbed if unappealed, but real exposure where the merits are finely balanced. Section seventy-three sidesteps it, because the original survives whatever happens. Costs follow unreasonable behaviour — a condition that plainly flunks the six tests, or a refusal of details that obviously comply.

On breach, the authority picks its weapon. The breach of condition notice is fast — comply within at least twenty-eight days, no appeal to the Secretary of State, judicial review your only challenge, and non-compliance is a criminal offence with an unlimited fine. The enforcement notice is slower but opens the full appeal, including the ground that asks for permission on the merits. The injunction is for the flagrant and urgent. They're not mutually exclusive. On timing, the enforcement window is now ten years for breaches from April 2024 on, the old periods running transitionally for earlier ones, with lawful development certificates to nail down immunity.

The gravest disputes are about implementation. You implement with a material operation before expiry — but under Whitley, works done in breach of condition aren't permitted by the permission read with its conditions, so they can't be lawful commencement. If the only pre-deadline works were unlawful, the permission was never implemented and it's lapsed. It turns on whether the breached condition was a true condition precedent: mere timing words with no prohibitory language didn't void thirty years of quarrying, but 'before any work is commenced' followed by something that 'shall be agreed' was a true precedent — and the permission was lost. The test is prohibitory language going to the heart of the permission.

The escapes are narrow. Whitley itself excused works where the scheme was approved before the deadline, and later cases rationalised that as where enforcement would be irrational or an abuse of power. But informal comfort won't do — planning is a comprehensive code, legitimate expectation faces a high threshold, and reassurance from a case officer is not a discharge. Interpretation runs on objective construction: read the permission as a whole, imply only with great restraint. The court won't rewrite a bad condition, or imply the restriction the authority forgot.
